# Systems and properties

FIXTURE: synthetic notes for tests, not teaching content.

A thermodynamic system is the quantity of matter or region of space chosen for careful study. Everything outside the system boundary is called the surroundings, and energy may cross between them. A closed system exchanges energy with its surroundings but never exchanges mass across the boundary. An isolated system exchanges neither energy nor mass, so its total energy remains constant forever.

Intensive properties such as pressure and temperature do not depend on the extent of the system. Extensive properties such as volume and internal energy scale directly with the amount of matter.

# Work and heat

The zeroth law states that two bodies in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium together. Temperature scales are established by assigning numerical values to reproducible fixed reference states. Work is energy transferred when a force acts through a displacement on the system boundary. Boundary work requires a moving boundary, as when a piston compresses gas inside a cylinder.

Heat transfer is energy crossing the boundary solely because of a temperature difference between regions. Adiabatic processes involve no heat transfer, although work interactions may still change internal energy.

# The first law

The first law expresses conservation of energy for every process that a closed system undergoes. Internal energy is a property, whereas heat and work are path functions that depend on the process. Specific heat measures the energy required to raise the temperature of unit mass by one degree. Enthalpy combines internal energy with the product of pressure and volume for convenient flow analysis.
